analysis.one_liner: Hands the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to Alaska for oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have handed the federal government's share of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain — the 1.5-million-acre "1002 Area" long closed to drilling — to the State of Alaska within 30 days, explicitly to speed up oil and gas development. Alaska would keep half the revenue from whatever it pumped, sending the other half to the U.S. Treasury, and oil produced there could not be exported. It never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to a large, currently off-limits area of the Arctic Refuge for drilling, and the State of Alaska would gain permanent title to the land plus 50% of all resource revenue. Supporters argued consumers would benefit from more domestic oil supply during the 2008 gas price spike, backed by the export ban.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers, plus Alaska's treasury

how_it_helps.text: It orders the Interior Department to transfer all federal rights to the 1002 Area — the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge — to Alaska within 30 days of enactment, explicitly to allow 'expeditious development' of oil and gas there.
Alaska would keep half of all revenue from developing the oil, gas, and other resources of the area, with the other half paid to the federal treasury.
Oil produced in the 1002 Area could not be exported from the United States, a nod to the bill's argument that the resource would serve domestic consumption.

analysis.who_pays: The public would permanently lose a federally protected wilderness area — the calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd and habitat for Arctic wildlife — and the federal government would give up full control of a public resource for a 50% revenue share. Any drilling revenue benefit to consumers would depend on future oil prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via lost wilderness protection

drawbacks.text: The transfer would permanently remove the Arctic Refuge Coastal Plain from federal protection, ending its status as a national wildlife refuge area where oil development is prohibited.
The 50% royalty condition would give the State of Alaska a direct financial stake in maximizing drilling in the transferred area, removing federal oversight over whether development happens at all.

The export ban added little protection for consumers: crude oil exports from the United States were already broadly prohibited under existing law at the time, so the bill's main 'domestic consumption' guarantee largely restated current policy.

Development of the Coastal Plain would threaten the calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd and other Arctic wildlife, and oil from new Arctic fields would take years to reach market, providing no relief during the 2008 price spike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a potential addition to domestic oil supply and revenue splits between Alaska and the federal treasury, but at the cost of permanently handing over a federal wilderness area that is the calving ground of the Porcupine caribou herd and habitat for other Arctic wildlife — a loss that could not be undone once the transfer happened. The revenue-sharing design also gave the state a direct financial stake in maximizing development. Given that the Coastal Plain was estimated to hold a modest share of national supply and would take years to bring online, the environmental cost weighed heavily against a small and delayed energy benefit; its death in committee preserved the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing until the 110th Congress ended, which kills any bill that was never taken up.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 23, 2008 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and the Foreign Affairs Committee.
On July 28, 2008 it was referred to the Natural Resources subcommittees on Energy and Mineral Resources and on Fisheries, Wildlife, and Oceans.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the last recorded action was the subcommittee referral.
The bill carried 52 cosponsors, all Republicans, but never advanced past committee referral before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Arctic Refuge Coastal Plain stayed under federal protection, and oil and gas companies did not gain access to it; ordinary citizens retained the public resource.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public's stake in the Arctic Refuge was preserved

for.name: Rep. Ralph M. Hall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the transfer of the Arctic Refuge Coastal Plain to Alaska for oil and gas development.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee (Chair Nick Rahall, D-WV)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its July 2008 referral; the record shows no committee action beyond sending it to subcommittees.

sides.party_line_note: All 52 cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and a Democratic-controlled House never took it up.

industries.note: The bill would open the Arctic Refuge Coastal Plain to oil and gas development by transferring federal land to Alaska with a mandate for 'expeditious development.' The export ban in the bill was largely redundant because crude oil exports were already broadly prohibited by existing law, so it imposed little real constraint on producers.
Alaska would receive title to the area and keep 50% of all resource revenue, giving the state government a large new income stream and a direct financial interest in maximum drilling.
The transfer would end federal protection of a pristine area of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge that currently cannot be leased for development, removing its value as protected public land.
